title: Adjusting Imports of Medium- and Heavy-Duty Vehicles, Medium- and Heavy-Duty Vehicle Parts, and Buses Into the United States
summary:
The United States will add new tariffs on imported medium- and heavy-duty trucks, key truck parts, and buses starting November 1, 2025. Most trucks and parts will face a 25% duty and buses a 10% duty. The stated aim is to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers, rebuild domestic production, and protect national security.

Who stands to benefit? U.S. makers of trucks, buses, and components could see a lift, along with workers in factories and foundries tied to these vehicles. The government says stronger homegrown supply chains will help the military and emergency services get the vehicles and parts they need in a crisis. Companies that assemble trucks or engines in the United States can apply for credits through 2030 to offset some parts costs, and older vehicles (25 years or more) are exempt. For products coming from Canada or Mexico under the regional trade pact, importers may be allowed to pay the duty only on the non‑U.S. content, once a verification process is in place. The policy also lines up with earlier actions on cars and parts and includes potential tariff adjustments for certain steel and aluminum producers in Canada or Mexico that support U.S. vehicle production.

Who might be negatively affected? Importers and foreign brands selling trucks, buses, and parts in the U.S. face higher costs. Fleet operators, public transit agencies, school districts, and small businesses that buy imported vehicles or rely on imported parts could see prices rise, at least in the short term. Higher equipment costs may ripple into freight rates and the price of goods moved by truck. Some U.S. manufacturers with global supply chains may need to rework sourcing to avoid penalties, especially since misreporting U.S. content can trigger the full 25% duty on the entire vehicle value until corrected. Trading partners could also push back, adding uncertainty for companies that buy or sell across borders.

Supporters argue the move will stabilize domestic market share at a higher level, spur investment, and add skilled jobs. Critics warn it could raise costs and slow adoption of newer vehicle technologies if parts become more expensive or scarce. The policy leaves room for future changes: the Commerce Department can add more parts to the tariff list, refine how content is measured, and recommend adjustments if conditions improve or new problems appear.
